title: Fact or Fiction
subtitle: The Stories, Checked
intro: He hated being called Teddy. He never said several of the things carved on plinths. And the bear in the cartoon that started a toy industry was not the bear most people picture. Fifteen questions separating the famous stories from the record.
heroAlt: Clifford Berryman's 1902 cartoon "Drawing the Line in Mississippi"
heroCredit: "Drawing the Line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

badge.title: Fact or Fiction

tiers.name: Believer
tiers.line: Half of what you know isn't so. Start here.

questions.prompt: How did Roosevelt feel about the nickname "Teddy"?
options: He loved it and used it himself
He disliked it and family never used it
He was indifferent
He invented it
questions.explanation: He disliked it. The family called him Teedie as a boy and Theodore as a man; Edith called him Theodore. "Teddy" was the public's and the newspapers', and one associate said the surest way to annoy him was to use it to his face.
questions.imageAlt: Seated three-quarter length portrait of Theodore Roosevelt
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, three-quarter length portrait, seated. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: The teddy bear came from a 1902 hunting trip. What actually happened?
options: Roosevelt shot a bear and regretted it
He refused to shoot a bear that had been captured and tied for him
He rescued an orphaned cub
He was attacked by a bear and survived
questions.explanation: On a Mississippi hunt his guides cornered and tied a bear so the president could shoot it. He refused — it was unsportsmanlike — though he did order the exhausted animal put out of its misery. Clifford Berryman's cartoon of the refusal is what launched the toy.
questions.imageAlt: Berryman's cartoon "Drawing the Line in Mississippi"
questions.credit: "Drawing the Line in Mississippi," Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: How did the bear in Berryman's cartoons change over time?
options: It stayed exactly the same
It became smaller and cuter, turning into a cub
It was dropped after a year
It became a grizzly
questions.explanation: The animal in the first drawing is a full-grown bear. Berryman kept redrawing it in later cartoons, and it shrank into the round-eyed cub everyone now pictures. The toy followed the cartoon, not the hunt.
questions.imageAlt: A later Clifford Berryman political cartoon featuring the bear
questions.credit: "To the Woods!" Clifford K. Berryman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: "Speak softly and carry a big stick." Where did Roosevelt say the phrase came from?
options: He coined it himself
He credited it to a West African proverb
It came from Lincoln
It was a Rough Rider saying
questions.explanation: He attributed it to a West African proverb when he used it publicly in 1901. The half everyone forgets is "speak softly" — he meant restraint backed by capability, not swagger.
questions.imageAlt: Chromolithograph print "A young head on old shoulders"
questions.credit: "A young head on old shoulders." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: The famous "Man in the Arena" passage comes from a speech given where?
options: Chicago, 1912
The Sorbonne in Paris, 1910
Osawatomie, Kansas, 1910
The White House, 1905
questions.explanation: From "Citizenship in a Republic," delivered at the Sorbonne on April 23, 1910, a year after he left office. The arena passage is a few sentences in a very long address about the duties of citizens.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, three-quarter length portrait, seated. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt is often quoted saying he could carve a judge with more backbone out of a banana. Did he?
options: Yes, in a letter to Henry Cabot Lodge
There is no reliable evidence he said it
Yes, in a public speech
Yes, but about a senator, not a judge
questions.explanation: It is the most quotable line attached to his frustration with Justice Holmes, and it cannot be traced to him. Its earliest appearance is in a 1932 biography of Holmes — decades later, in indirect speech, citing no manuscript. A similar phrase was already circulating in the press by 1900.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, three-quarter length portrait, seated. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Did Roosevelt charge up San Juan Hill on horseback at the head of his men?
options: Yes, exactly as the paintings show
He was mounted, but the hill his regiment took was Kettle Hill
He was not present at the battle
He led the charge on foot the whole way
questions.explanation: He was mounted — officers' horses had made the crossing when the troopers' had not — but the Rough Riders' charge went up Kettle Hill, part of the same San Juan Heights. He dismounted near the crest where wire blocked the way.
questions.imageAlt: Painting of the charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill
questions.credit: Charge of the Rough Riders at San Juan Hill, reproduction of a painting. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Several celebrated photographs of Roosevelt's Badlands adventures are what?
options: Documentary photographs taken as events happened
Re-creations staged afterwards with friends posing
Later paintings mistaken for photographs
Composites of several negatives
questions.explanation: The best-known image of Roosevelt guarding the captured boat thieves was posed after the fact, with Sewall, Dow and an unidentified man standing in as the prisoners. It is a good picture and an honest one only if you say so.
questions.imageAlt: Staged photograph of Roosevelt guarding the boat thieves
questions.credit: "T.R. guarding the boat thieves" — a re-creation staged after the fact. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Was Roosevelt's famous 1912 line “I'm as fit as a bull moose” the origin of the party's nickname?
options: Yes
No, the moose came from a newspaper cartoon
No, it was Taft's insult
No, it was a Progressive Party committee decision
questions.explanation: Roosevelt told an inquiring reporter “I'm as fit as a bull moose” and had used the comparison for years to describe his own vigour, and the press attached it to the Progressive Party. That much is straightforward — unusually for this quiz.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and Hiram Johnson after the Progressive Party nomination
questions.credit: Roosevelt and Johnson after nomination. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Was Roosevelt the youngest person ever elected president?
options: Yes
No — he was the youngest to hold the office, but reached it through succession
No, that was Lincoln
Yes, at forty-two
questions.explanation: He became president at forty-two, younger than anyone before or since, but by succession after McKinley's assassination. The youngest man ever *elected* was John F. Kennedy, at forty-three.
questions.imageAlt: Vice President Roosevelt at McKinley's swearing in, March 1901
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt at the swearing in of President McKinley, March 1901. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt is said to have offered to raise "an entire regiment of cowboys" for the government in 1886. Is that his phrase?
options: Yes, from a letter to Henry Cabot Lodge
No — it comes from a newspaper speculating about what he might do
Yes, from a speech in Medora
No, it was invented in the 1950s
questions.explanation: The phrase appears in quotation marks in more than one modern biography, but it traces to a Bismarck newspaper reporting that it was "confidently believed" Roosevelt *would* offer such a regiment. What he actually wrote to Lodge was "some companies of horse riflemen."
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt mounted in ranch clothes near Medora
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in ranch costume. Photograph by T. W. Ingersoll. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How long did the men who stole Roosevelt's boat actually serve?
options: Three years
Twenty-five months
Six months
They were acquitted
questions.explanation: Twenty-five months. A widely read biography says three years, but the local newspaper of the day and several later historians agree on twenty-five months. Small discrepancies like this survive for a century because people quote each other rather than the record.
questions.credit: Dickinson, N.D., 1883. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: "Old Four Eyes" is the nickname most often attached to Roosevelt's Badlands years. What did people actually call him?
options: Old Four Eyes, exactly that
The four-eyed dude
The Colonel
Mr. Roosevelt only
questions.explanation: Contemporaries used the blunter phrase — "the four-eyed dude," or in one barroom, simply "Four Eyes." The tidier "Old Four Eyes" is largely a later coinage, smoothed by retelling.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in his first buckskin suit
questions.credit: "Theodore Roosevelt in his first buckskins." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Did Roosevelt really keep a bullet in his chest after the 1912 assassination attempt?
options: No, it was removed that night
Yes, for the remaining seven years of his life
No, the bullet never reached him
Yes, but only for a few months
questions.explanation: True. Surgeons judged the risk of removing it greater than the risk of leaving it, and he carried it until he died. He also finished the speech first, having reasoned aloud that he was not coughing blood.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt with Rough Rider veterans during the Bull Moose campaign
questions.credit: T.R. with Rough Rider veterans during the Bull Moose campaign, Chicago. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What is the most reliable way to check whether Roosevelt said something?
options: If it appears in quotation marks in a modern biography
Trace it to his own letters, speeches or books with a date
If several websites agree
If it sounds like him
questions.explanation: Biographies quote each other, and a phrase in quotation marks is not proof of authorship. The test is a primary source with a date — a letter, a printed speech, a book. Sounding like him is precisely how the fakes spread.
questions.imageAlt: Photograph taken by a family member in the library at Sagamore Hill
questions.credit: Taken by one of the family in the library at Sagamore Hill. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.
